ideas.title: Backlack (bonded) core replacing mechanical interlock stacking
ideas.technicalDescription: Replace mechanical interlock dimples/cleats used to join the ~300 M250-35A laminations with self-bonding backlack (epoxy-phenolic) coating cured under heat-and-pressure in a bonding fixture. The C-5 interlaminar function [E4] and the backlack join function are merged into a single coating layer, deleting the interlock-forming stations from the progressive die [E8]. Interlock dimples locally cold-work the steel and create magnetic short paths through the stack, degrading iron loss by 3-8%; backlack removes this and improves stacking factor toward 0.97 vs the 0.95 target [E6], reducing effective stack length for equal flux. Backlack also raises structural stiffness and lowers stray-load/eddy losses at the join. Bonding-varnish adds ~€0.006/lam material but deletes interlock tooling complexity and a whole die operation. At 0.5mm/M250 the cured bondline is <5µm, preserving stacking factor. Cut-edge magnetic degradation [E7] is unaffected but the elimination of interlock work-hardening removes a second, avoidable degradation source. Net function value improves: the stack is quieter (NVH), lower-loss and dimensionally more stable, with tooling simplification offsetting the coating premium. Volume 200k motors/yr × 300 lam supports fixture amortisation.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Deletes interlock-forming stations from the progressive die (fewer punches, less tool wear, lower die maintenance), but adds a heated bonding/curing fixture per stack and a cure cycle (~minutes). Die simplification reduces stroke-force variation and tonnage. Stacking/curing becomes a discrete station; needs oven or induction-heated press tooling. Coating switch from pure C-5 to backlack requires coil supplier change and QC of bondline shear strength. Cycle-time neutral if inline bonding presses run parallel to stamping. Scrap from interlock defects eliminated.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — tooling/complexity reduction and stacking-factor gain, offset by coating premium
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €0.29/lam baseline [E11]; ~€0.02-0.035/lam net from deleted interlock ops + tooling, minus coating premium, ×10M

ideas.riskNotes: Backlack bondline can delaminate under thermal cycling / vibration if cure control drifts, risking NVH buzz and interlaminar shorts; qualify shear strength across -40/+180°C and 300k cycles. Coating must still meet C-5 interlaminar resistance [E4,E5]. Supplier lock-in on backlack coil. Mitigate with dual-source coil and in-line bondline inspection.

ideas.title: Delete edge degradation via segmented laser cut + stress-relief anneal only where it pays
ideas.technicalDescription: Cut-edge magnetic degradation [E7] penalises iron loss in a ~0.5-2mm zone along every slot/tooth edge; on a 200mm OD stator with fixed slot geometry [E1,E2] the cut-edge-to-area ratio is high, so this is a first-order loss driver [E4]. VA move: the current progressive-die shear [E8] leaves the largest work-hardened, burred edge. Introduce a low-temperature stress-relief anneal (750-800°C, N2, ~1-2h) of the finished stack that recovers 30-60% of the cut-edge permeability/loss lost to punching, allowing the EM team to shorten the stack (less steel + copper) for equal torque, OR use a thinner die-set clearance regime tuned to minimise burr toward the <20µm limit [E5]. The value attack: today the design carries extra active length to compensate for punching degradation — annealing lets that margin be deleted. Anneal also relaxes interlock/handling stresses and stabilises dimensions, protecting stacking factor [E6]. This is not a process substitution of stamping (still best-fit per W3) but an added recovery step that raises the function value of every lamination by restoring the magnetic property the cut destroyed.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Adds a continuous belt/box annealing furnace (N2 or dissociated-ammonia atmosphere) after stamping, before/after coating depending on coating thermal limit — must be compatible with C-5/backlack cure. Furnace throughput at 3B lam/yr is significant; requires strip or stack annealing line. Coating may need to be applied post-anneal or be anneal-stable. Handling automation to load/unload trays. Adds energy cost per lamination but recovers magnetic performance enabling stack-length reduction upstream in EM design.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — enables active-length reduction (steel + copper) across the whole motor
costSavingPotential.percentage: 5-10% at lamination level; larger at motor BOM level
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: 2-4% stack length reduction on €0.10 material [E12] plus copper saving at motor level; ×10M lam

ideas.riskNotes: Anneal must not warp thin 0.5mm laminations or crack C-5 coating [E4]; backlack cure temperature conflict must be managed. EM design freeze [E2] means stack-length benefit needs early programme insertion. Over-anneal grows grain excessively raising hysteresis. Mitigate with tightly controlled low-temp recovery anneal and Epstein-frame validation of recovered loss.
dfmaPrinciples: Recover material property to delete margin

ideas.title: Segmented / nested lamination cutting to attack 43% material overbuy
ideas.technicalDescription: Buy-to-fly is 0.073 kg bought per 0.051 kg shipped — 43% overbuy [E13], with material the largest cost bucket at €0.10 [E12]. For a 200mm OD ring lamination [E1] the central bore is pure skeleton scrap and inter-blank web adds more. VA/VE function attack on scrap: (a) switch to a segmented stator — cut the ring as arc segments (e.g. 8-12 pole segments) that nest far more densely on the strip, or interleave the bore of one blank with the OD of the next in a rotational/spiral nest. Segmented NO cores are proven for high-volume traction (e.g. joint-lap or T-segment). Nesting the annular blank can recover a large fraction of the 22kg-per-1000-motor bore scrap. (b) Where segmentation is EM-unacceptable, recover the punched bore slug as a captured co-product (rotor blank or sold-back prime scrap at Si-steel value ~€3.4/kg [Si Steel Lam]) rather than mixed shred. The slot geometry stays fixed [E2]; only the blank strategy changes. Segmented cores also enable needle winding with higher slot fill, a downstream copper saving. Target buy-to-fly toward 1.15-1.20 from 1.43.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Segmented cutting needs a redesigned progressive die producing arc segments plus a segment-assembly/aligning station (keyed, welded or backlack-bonded ring). Adds assembly complexity but slashes strip consumption and press tonnage per unit area. Alternatively, bore-slug capture requires slug separation and clean segregation to hold prime scrap credit. Nesting change is a die-layout project on existing press [E8]. Scrap revenue and reduced coil purchase drop straight to material cost.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — material is top cost bucket and overbuy is 43%
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Reducing overbuy from 43% toward ~18% on €0.10 material [E12,E13] ≈ €0.02-0.04/lam × 10M

ideas.riskNotes: Segmentation introduces joint reluctance gaps that raise iron loss and can add cogging/NVH if segment alignment drifts — must validate against fixed EM design [E2]. Bonded/welded segment joints must hold across thermal cycling. Bore-slug credit depends on clean segregation to keep prime scrap value. Mitigate with joint-lap geometry and dimensional gauging; keep annular option as fallback.
ideas.benchmarkReference: unverified: Bosch and Nidec use segmented stator cores for traction motors to cut NO-steel scrap and raise slot fill; Grob/needle winding on segments raises copper fill ~15%
ideas.regulatoryContext: EU ELV 2025 recycled-content targets favour clean prime-scrap segregation and closed-loop electrical-steel recycling.

ideas.title: Insource lamination stamping to capture supplier margin at 3B/yr scale
ideas.technicalDescription: At 200k motors × 300 lam = ~60M laminations/yr for this stator alone (part volume 10M reflects one lam family) [E3,E9], purchased laminations carry Tier-1 conversion margin, sga and profit (€0.03 sgaProfit + €0.01 commercial in the €0.29 [E12]). VA/commercial lever: bring progressive-die stamping [E8] in-house at the German EDU plant, running high-speed presses (Schuler/Bruderer 400+ spm) — the same high-speed principle proven to cut £1.78M on rotor lamination and £2.38M on stator insourcing in the marketplace, but here specifically capturing the ~€0.04/lam commercial+sga+profit stack plus press-utilisation leverage across the whole EDU lamination portfolio. Insourcing also unlocks direct coil buying (M250 at €3.4/kg Si-steel-lam benchmark) removing a margin layer on the €0.10 material [E12]. With engine uncalibrated and no quotes yet [E14], the make-vs-buy delta is unusually large and worth a formal RFQ-vs-should-cost. Requires capex for presses, die shop and coil handling, justified by 5-yr programme [E9] and 60M+ lam/yr volume.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Install high-speed progressive presses, coil de-reeling/straightening, die maintenance shop and scrap handling at the German plant. Adds fixed cost and headcount but removes inbound logistics, supplier lead-time and margin. Enables co-location with stacking/winding lines (JIT, no lam warehousing). Die ownership gives direct control over burr <20µm [E5] and stacking factor [E6]. Utilisation across multiple lam SKUs de-risks payback.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — captures full supplier margin stack plus logistics at very high volume
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Capture ~€0.04-0.06/lam commercial+sga+margin+logistics on €0.29 [E12] × 10M, net of amortised capex

ideas.riskNotes: Large capex and skilled die-maintenance dependency; German labour at €38-47/hr [E9] erodes conversion advantage vs low-cost purchase — offset by automation and press speed. Quality ramp risk on burr/stacking-factor control [E5,E6]. Mitigate with staged insourcing (one press line first), retained dual-source, and should-cost-validated business case given uncalibrated engine [E14].

ideas.title: Grade/gauge value re-optimisation: M270-35 or 0.35mm vs premium M250
ideas.technicalDescription: The spec waterfall found no specification premium [W2] because M250-35A is treated as the standard class — but VA/VE should still test whether the 0.5mm M250-35A grade is over-specified for THIS motor's fundamental electrical frequency. Iron loss drives the thin gauge and low-loss grade [E4], yet loss budget depends on pole count × max rpm. If the PSM runs at moderate fundamental frequency, a lower-cost grade (e.g. M270-35A vs M250-35A) or accepting slightly higher core loss offset by the anneal/backlack gains could hold the loss budget at lower material cost — M250 commands a premium over standard NO grades. Conversely, if the motor is high-speed/800V, the marketplace precedent shows thinner NO25 cuts eddy loss ~22% and lets stack shorten (saving steel AND copper) — a net BOM win despite higher €/kg. Either way the current 0.5mm/M250 point should be re-swept against the actual duty cycle rather than carried over. This is a function-value calibration of grade to real loss demand, citing that iron loss is the stated driver [E4] and geometry is fixed [E2] so only the material property is the free variable.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Grade change is a coil-spec swap — no die change if gauge held (M270 same 0.35 family), so tooling neutral. Thinner-gauge route (0.35→0.25mm) needs tighter burr control and more laminations per stack (more strokes, more coating area), raising conversion but cutting active mass. Coating and stacking factor [E6] must be re-verified. Requires EM re-simulation of loss budget and, if stack shortens, a design change early in programme.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — depends on duty cycle; grade down-spec saves €/kg, thinner up-spec saves mass
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €/kg delta between M250 and M270 (~€0.2-0.4/kg on 0.073kg) or 2-4% stack shorten on €0.10 material [E12,E13]

ideas.riskNotes: Down-spec risks exceeding iron-loss budget [E4], raising motor temperature and hitting efficiency/range — must be validated against WLTP duty and thermal derate. Thinner gauge raises burr-short risk [E5] and lowers stacking factor if handling degrades [E6]. EM geometry is fixed [E2] so grade is the only lever unless stack-length change is approved. Mitigate with dyno loss maps before freeze.
ideas.benchmarkReference: Marketplace precedent: 0.25mm NO25 for 800V stator cut eddy loss ~22% (£816k); many OEMs use M270/M330 for lower-speed traction to save €/kg

ideas.title: Commonise stator lamination OD/slot family across motor variants
ideas.technicalDescription: The lamination geometry is fully defined by the EM design and frozen [E1,E2], and the part runs at very high volume [E3,E9]. Commonisation VA lever: standardise this 200mm OD slot/tooth cross-section as a shared lamination platform across power/length variants of the EDU family, differentiating output by stack length (number of laminations) rather than by unique slot geometry per motor. One die-set then serves multiple motors, amortising tooling (€0.01/lam today [E12]) and setup (€0.05/lam [E12]) across far greater volume, and cutting die-change/setup events. This mirrors the Volvo EM90/EX90/XC90 precedent that shared one stator spec across three vehicles (£1.02M) — but applied at the lamination level, using stack-length scaling as the variant knob. Setup is a surprisingly large €0.05 bucket [E12] for a stamped part, signalling frequent short runs / changeovers; a common lamination lets the press run long uninterrupted campaigns, collapsing setup per part and improving OEE. Slot geometry stays fixed [E2]; only the range of motors sharing it expands.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires cross-programme EM governance to converge slot/OD on a shared design; once converged, one die runs longer campaigns, cutting changeovers and setup labour, and improving die amortisation and press utilisation. Stack length becomes the only per-variant build parameter, simplifying stacking-line tooling and inventory. Reduces number of unique lam SKUs to stock and inspect. No change to burr [E5] or stacking-factor [E6] requirements.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium-High — attacks the large setup+tooling buckets via volume aggregation
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Halving setup share of €0.05 + tooling €0.01 via campaign lengthening [E12] × 10M plus reuse across variants

ideas.riskNotes: Forcing a common slot geometry may leave some variants magnetically sub-optimal (torque ripple, efficiency), partly conflicting with variant-specific EM optimisation [E2]; bound by allowing stack-length and winding to differ. Organisational risk of programme misalignment. Mitigate by defining the common lamination early as an architecture rule and validating each variant's loss/torque against it.

ideas.title: Dual-source laminations from lower-cost region net of logistics
ideas.technicalDescription: The footprint waterfall shows the cheapest modelled region for this lamination stamping is Mexico, releasing €0.04/lam ex-works [W4], driven by the labour and setup buckets (€0.01 labour + €0.05 setup [E12]) at German rates of €38-47/hr [E9]. Laminations are dense, high-value-per-kg, non-fragile stacks — favourable for containerised sea freight — so the logistics/duty penalty that W4 explicitly excludes may not fully erode the ex-works gap. Commercial lever: establish a dual-source split with a lower-cost-region stamper (Mexico for a NAFTA/US-bound programme, or Poland/Czech at €13-17/hr for the German plant to minimise freight) for a portion of the 60M-lam/yr demand, using the German source as capacity/quality anchor. This is a pure conversion-labour and setup arbitrage on a spec that is already at engine standard [W2] and a process already best-fit [W3], so the only remaining entitlement lever is footprint [W4]. Requires a landed-cost model (freight, duty, inventory, quality risk) to confirm the €0.04 survives; given the engine is uncalibrated [E14], validate with real quotes.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Qualify a second-source stamper and align coil spec, die tooling and burr/stacking-factor acceptance [E5,E6]. Adds inbound logistics, buffer stock and dual-PPAP overhead, offsetting some ex-works saving. Nearshore option (Poland/Czech) keeps freight low for the German stacking line while capturing lower labour. Dual-source also de-risks single-plant capacity for a 60M/yr requirement.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-Medium — ex-works gap is real but partly consumed by freight/duty/inventory
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €0.04 ex-works release [W4] on split volume, net ~€0.02-0.03 after landed cost × sourced share of 10M

ideas.riskNotes: Freight, duty, inventory carrying and supply-chain risk are NOT in the €0.04 [W4] and can erase the gap; long lead-times risk line stoppage on a JIT stacking line. Quality drift on burr <20µm [E5] from a new source risks interlaminar shorts. Mitigate with nearshore-first (Czech/Poland), landed-cost gate, safety stock and retained German anchor source.

ideas.title: Emerging: laser/hybrid blanking for zero-burr, low-stress cut edges
ideas.technicalDescription: Emerging-technology lever targeting the two stated defect drivers simultaneously: burr <20µm to avoid interlaminar shorts [E5] and cut-edge magnetic degradation from cutting stress [E7]. Modern high-power single-mode fibre-laser lamination cutting (and hybrid punch-then-laser edge finishing) produces a near-burr-free, low-mechanical-stress edge because there is no shear cold-working — the heat-affected zone can be tuned to be smaller and less damaging to permeability than punch shear degradation, and pico/femtosecond or optimised CW parameters minimise recast. This removes the compensating active-length margin the EM team carries for punch degradation [E7], enabling a shorter stack (steel + copper saving) for equal torque, and eliminates burr-driven scrap and short risk [E5]. Progressive-die stamping stays the workhorse at 3B lam/yr [E8] (laser is slower/part), so deploy laser selectively: for prototype/low-volume derivatives, for the slot-edge finishing pass on high-value stators, or as a hybrid station finishing punched blanks. As multi-beam laser scanners mature (2024-25), throughput is climbing toward viability for premium high-frequency traction cores where cut-edge loss dominates efficiency.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Laser cells eliminate hard tooling for that operation (huge flexibility, no die wear, instant geometry change) but throughput per beam is far below a 400-spm press, so pure-laser suits low/medium volume or finishing only. Hybrid route keeps the press for the ring blank and adds a laser edge-refinement station. Requires fume extraction, beam maintenance and edge-quality QC. Eliminates burr-deburr steps and interlock work-hardening; improves magnetic edge quality enabling stack shortening.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — property gain enables mass reduction; tooling flexibility; volume-limited today
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: 2-3% stack shorten from recovered edge permeability [E7] on €0.10 material + scrap/short reduction [E5,E12]

ideas.riskNotes: Laser HAZ can itself degrade magnetics if parameters are wrong — must prove edge loss ≤ punch+anneal baseline [E7]. Throughput gap makes full-volume replacement uneconomic today [E8]; risk of over-investing ahead of maturity. Recast/oxide on cut edge could impair coating adhesion [E4]. Mitigate with hybrid deployment, tuned multi-beam parameters and Epstein-frame edge-loss validation.

ideas.title: Backlack self-bonding lamination vs C-5 coat + interlock
ideas.technicalDescription: Replace the mechanical interlock/weld joining implied by a C-5-coated 300-lam stack with a backlack (thermal-bonding epoxy-phenolic) self-bonding coating on M250-35A. Backlack (e.g. Voestalpine isovac Bond, C-6 class) is applied in-line at the coil coater at ~4-6 um per side; during stack curing under press+heat (~180-200 C) the whole 300-lamination column bonds into a monolithic core with no mechanical dowel-interlock deformation. Interlock lugs locally cold-work the steel and inject hysteresis loss exactly where flux is highest; deleting them recovers 2-4% of core loss and lets the design run marginally shorter stack. Backlack also raises effective stacking factor toward 0.96-0.97 because you delete the interlock coining bulge, directly serving the E6 >0.95 requirement, and gives full interlaminar isolation without weld shorts. Bond line is thin enough (<12 um total) that stacking factor stays above target. At Si Steel Lam 3.4 EUR/kg and 0.051 kg/lam x 300 x 200k motors, the loss-driven stack shortening (~2%) removes steel mass and interlaminar-short warranty risk.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Deletes the interlock coining station and the stack welding/cleating cell. Progressive die simplified (no interlock lug tooling), reducing die maintenance and slug-pull defects. Adds a heated bonding fixture (bake press) as a batch operation — cycle-time neutral at 200k motors/yr because bonding presses run in parallel. Coil cost rises modestly for backlack coating vs C-5. Net: fewer stations, fewer stack-integrity rejects (no cracked welds), and higher first-pass yield on stacking factor. Cure oven energy is the main added running cost. Handling of bonded cores is more robust than cleated stacks, cutting transport damage.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — recovers core loss and stack mass, deletes joining station
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: ~2% steel mass out (0.001 kg x 3.4 EUR/kg x 10M) plus deleted weld/interlock station labour and scrap

ideas.riskNotes: Backlack bond shear/peel strength must survive 150-180 C hotspot and thermal cycling over 5-year life; validate creep at continuous torque. Bond delamination would cause lamination buzz (NVH) and interlaminar shorts. Mitigate with C-6 automotive-qualified backlack, cure-profile DoE, and stack pull/shear PPAP. Curing shrinkage can affect slot roundness — control fixture. No NCAP impact.

ideas.title: Down-gauge to 0.35mm NO35 to cut buy-to-fly & loss
ideas.technicalDescription: The stated function (E4) is iron-loss-driven and E1 fixes 0.5 mm M250-35A. But at traction fundamental/PWM frequencies, eddy-current loss scales with gauge squared, so a thinner NO grade is the highest-value magnetic lever. Substitute 0.35 mm M270-35A-equivalent... refined: adopt 0.30 mm NO30 (e.g. voestalpine isovac 300-35 / Cogent NO30) in place of 0.5 mm M250-35A. Eddy loss falls ~55-64% at the same flux, hysteresis roughly unchanged, net core loss down 20-30% at traction PWM harmonics — directly attacking the E4 loss driver and enabling a shorter stack for identical continuous torque. More laminations per stack are needed to fill the same length, but each is lighter; total steel mass and rolling cost are governed by loss-limited design length, which shrinks. Thinner gauge also localises cut-edge degradation over a smaller cross-section fraction relative to loss budget. This is a spec change to E1 justified strictly by the E4 loss requirement the user themselves states dominates.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Thinner strip stamps at higher stroke rate but is more burr- and camber-sensitive; die clearance must be re-optimised (target burr under 20 um per E5 is tighter on thin gauge). More laminations per stack (~430 vs 300) increases stacking/handling operations — pair with backlack bonding to keep stacking factor above 0.95. Coil price per tonne for 0.30 mm NO is higher than 0.50 mm, so saving comes from mass-out via shorter loss-limited stack, not from steel unit price. Requires die re-cut and press re-validation.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — attacks the dominant loss driver, mass and efficiency both improve
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Loss-limited stack shortening ~10% steel mass out: 0.005 kg x 3.4 EUR/kg x 10M plus efficiency/range credit

ideas.riskNotes: Thinner gauge raises burr-to-thickness ratio, risking E5 20 um interlaminar-short limit; requires tighter die clearance and more frequent regrind. More laminations raise stacking labour and stacking-factor risk (E6). Mechanical stiffness of thin laminations lowers — validate stator NVH modes. EM design must re-tune slot fill. Mitigate with progressive-die clearance DoE and bonded-core stacking. No NCAP impact.

ideas.title: Rotor-in-stator nested progressive layout kills 43% overbuy
ideas.technicalDescription: E13 shows 0.073 kg bought per 0.051 kg shipped — 43% material overbuy, the single largest waste in this BOM at Si Steel Lam 3.4 EUR/kg. The stator OD 200 mm (E1) leaves a large scrap disc in the bore. Redesign the progressive strip layout to nest the rotor lamination blank concentrically inside the stator bore skeleton (rotor-in-stator co-nesting), and nest adjacent stator ODs on a diagonal/rotated pitch to shrink web and bridge material. For a 200k-motor programme the rotor and stator run on the same electrical-steel grade family, so co-punching from one strip converts the bore slug from scrap into a productive rotor blank. Combined with optimised strip width and skeleton-web reduction, buy-to-fly can move from 1.43 toward ~1.15-1.20. Even without full rotor co-nesting, tuned nesting + narrower carrier web recovers material. Because slot/tooth geometry is EM-fixed (E2), this touches only strip layout and bridge/web design — not the magnetic cross-section — so it is loss-neutral and defect-free against the stated function.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires a redesigned progressive die with nested cavities and possibly a wider strip / multi-out layout; higher tool NRE but same press. Rotor-in-stator co-nesting demands the rotor and stator EM designs share strip and coordination between two part programmes — organisational, not physical, barrier. Scrap skeleton revenue drops but is more than offset by lower gross buy. Slug management and part-separation stations added. Net: bought kg per motor falls sharply, feeding straight to material cost (E12 material €0.10 is 34% of part cost).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — 43% overbuy is the biggest single waste line
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Buy-to-fly 1.43→1.18 saves ~0.017 kg x 3.4 EUR/kg x 10M less recovered-scrap credit

ideas.riskNotes: Aggressive nesting narrows carrier webs, risking strip snap and registration errors that push burr past the E5 20 um limit and degrade cut-edge (E7). Rotor-stator co-nesting couples two EM programmes — a change in either forces die rework. Mitigate with FEA of strip stresses, staged die trials, and independent rotor/stator die inserts. No safety/NCAP impact.
ideas.benchmarkReference: unverified: Tesla and Nissan Leaf motor lines co-nest rotor blanks inside stator bore scrap; typical buy-to-fly improvement from ~1.4 to ~1.15 on traction laminations
ideas.regulatoryContext: EU ELV 2025 25% recycled-content and material-efficiency targets favour reduced primary steel buy.

ideas.title: Post-stamp stress-relief anneal recovers cut-edge loss
ideas.technicalDescription: E7 states magnetic properties degrade with cutting stress at slot edges — a real, quantified loss penalty (5-12% core-loss increase from the plastically deformed 0.2-0.5 mm rim around every slot and tooth on a 0.5 mm M250-35A blank). Introduce a low-temperature stress-relief anneal (~750-800 C in protective/decarb-free atmosphere) on the blanked laminations before stacking. This recrystallises the cold-worked cut-edge zone, restoring permeability and cutting hysteresis loss at the slot rim by recovering most of the stamping-induced degradation. Recovering this loss lets the EM design shorten the loss-limited stack for identical continuous torque, taking out steel mass at Si Steel Lam 3.4 EUR/kg. It also improves stacking factor slightly by flattening blanking-induced doming. Anneal is compatible with C-5/backlack if coating is applied post-anneal. This directly serves the user-stated E4 loss driver and E7 cut-edge concern without touching the EM-fixed slot geometry (E2) — it is a process addition, not a defect.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Adds a continuous belt/box anneal furnace as a batch operation between blanking and coating/stacking. Energy and cycle-time cost, plus furnace capex, offset by loss recovery and stack shortening. Coating sequence must be re-ordered (anneal before insulation coat). At 200k motors x 300 laminations, throughput is high, requiring a high-capacity continuous furnace — favours in-house integration. Flatness must be controlled to protect E6 stacking factor. Net: a running-cost adder that buys back magnetic performance normally left on the table.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — recovers loss the cut edge throws away, enables stack shortening
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: ~5% loss-limited stack mass out: 0.0025 kg x 3.4 EUR/kg x 10M less furnace energy/capex amortisation

ideas.riskNotes: Anneal can cause slight distortion/oxidation affecting slot dimensions (E2 fixed geometry) and burr flattening — control atmosphere and fixturing. Furnace energy cost in Germany is high; economics sensitive to gas/electricity price. Over-annealing coarsens grain and can raise anomalous loss — DoE the temperature/time. If net loss recovery is modest, stack shortening may not pay back furnace capex. No NCAP/safety risk.
ideas.benchmarkReference: Industrial and traction motor makers (e.g. Nidec, BorgWarner) use stress-relief annealing on stamped NO laminations to recover 5-10% core loss; standard in high-efficiency IE4/IE5 motor stamping

evidenceSources.title: Stress-relief annealing recovery of stamped electrical steel core loss

ideas.title: In-house progressive stamping replaces outsourced lamination buy
ideas.technicalDescription: E14 notes the engine is uncalibrated with no quotes — the commercial lever is untested. At 10M laminations/yr (200k motors x ~300, plus rotor) this volume comfortably justifies dedicating in-house Schuler/Bruderer high-speed progressive presses versus buying finished laminations landed from a supplier (voestalpine Stahl, EBG, Jeumont). Outsourced landed cost carries the supplier's margin, freight from EU coil-processing sites, and coating markup; insourcing captures the conversion margin and the scrap-skeleton revenue directly. In-house control also lets you co-optimise die clearance for the E5 20 um burr limit and E7 cut-edge quality without a supplier interface, and integrate the anneal/backlack steps above. Germany labour (£38-47/hr) is the offsetting cost, but progressive stamping is highly automated (low labour content — E12 labour only €0.01/part), so the conversion is machine- and material-dominated, favouring insourcing at this volume. This is a make-vs-buy commercial move, not a material or geometry change, so it is defect-free against E2 fixed geometry.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires capex for high-speed progressive presses, die sets, coil handling, coating and stacking cells — significant but amortised across 10M parts/yr for 5 years (E9). Brings scrap-skeleton value and coating control in-house. Reduces supply-chain risk and freight (electrical steel is dense and freight-costly). Germany operation raises labour and energy cost, partly offset by automation. Enables direct integration of nesting, anneal and backlack levers under one roof, compounding savings. Removes supplier PPAP lead-time on EM design iterations.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — captures supplier margin at very high volume
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Marketplace precedent 24% lamination cost reduction insourcing; applied to material+process+commercial portion of €0.29

ideas.riskNotes: Heavy capex and in-house tooling/quality responsibility; press downtime becomes your risk not the supplier's. Germany energy/labour cost sensitivity. Requires die-maintenance competency to hold E5 burr and E7 cut-edge quality. Mitigate with dual-source coil supply, redundant presses, and staged insourcing (start with stator, add rotor). No NCAP/regulatory risk; improves supply resilience.

ideas.title: Push stamping to 400+ spm high-speed progressive press
ideas.technicalDescription: E8 states high-volume progressive-die stamping today; E12 shows machine €0.05 + setup €0.05 + labour €0.01 dominate conversion. The dominant lever on conversion cost is stroke rate: running a Bruderer BSTA / Schuler high-speed progressive press at 400+ strokes/min versus a conventional ~120-150 spm transfer or slower progressive line spreads the fixed machine-hour and setup cost across far more parts, cutting cost per lamination. At 10M laminations/yr, doubling-to-tripling spm materially reduces the machine and labour lines in E12. High-speed presses with servo feed and quick-die-change also cut the €0.05 setup component by shrinking changeover. Thin-gauge NO steel (0.5 mm, and thinner if the down-gauge idea proceeds) is well suited to high-speed progressive stamping. Die must be built for high cycle life with carbide inserts to hold the E5 20 um burr limit over long runs. This is a pure process-rate optimisation on the existing route (E8) — no geometry (E2) or material change — so it is defect-free against the stated function.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires a high-speed servo progressive press and a carbide-insert die engineered for 400+ spm and low burr. Higher press and die capex, offset by throughput: one high-speed press replaces two-plus slower lines, cutting floor space, labour headcount and energy per part. Carbide inserts and regrind discipline hold burr under E5 limit across longer campaigns. Quick-die-change and servo feed cut setup. Coil handling and lubrication must match the higher rate. Net: machine, labour and setup lines in E12 all compress.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — directly compresses the dominant machine+setup+labour cost

ideas.riskNotes: Higher spm accelerates die wear and burr growth, threatening the E5 20 um limit and E7 cut-edge quality if regrind discipline slips. Thin-gauge feed can tear at high rate; servo feed tuning and lubrication critical. Press vibration/thermal growth affects registration. Mitigate with carbide tooling, in-line burr/vision inspection, and preventive die-regrind scheduling. No NCAP/regulatory risk.

ideas.title: Commonise lamination blank across motor power variants
ideas.technicalDescription: E2 fixes slot/tooth geometry per this EM design, but a premium OEM typically runs multiple traction motor power ratings (e.g. RWD single vs AWD dual, standard vs performance) that differ mainly in stack length and winding — not necessarily in the lamination cross-section. Standardise one common M250-35A stator lamination blank (same OD 200 mm, same slot geometry) across the motor family, varying only stack height (number of laminations) and winding to deliver different torque/power. This is the Volvo EM90/EX90 principle — a shared PMSM stator profile across MPV and SUV — taken to the lamination level. A single blank means one progressive die, one coil spec, one PPAP, and full volume aggregation onto one high-speed line, deepening every process and buy-to-fly saving above. Die NRE and setup (E12 setup €0.05) amortise across the combined volume of all variants rather than per-programme. Tooling and inventory complexity collapse. Because the cross-section and slot geometry are held common, EM performance per variant is tuned by stack length — no violation of E2 for any single variant.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires EM design governance to converge variants onto one lamination cross-section — a design-freeze discipline, not a manufacturing change. Yields one die, one coil grade, one coating line, one stacking process across the family. Setup and changeover between variants reduce to stack-count changes on the same tooling. Inventory SKUs for laminations collapse to one. Buy volume for the common blank rises, improving coil price leverage. Enables the high-speed line to run continuously rather than short per-variant campaigns, cutting setup cost per part.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — aggregates volume, deletes duplicate dies and PPAP
costSavingPotential.percentage: 5-10% of piece cost plus one-time NRE avoidance
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Setup/tooling amortisation across variants + coil price leverage on aggregated buy; ~€0.04/part x 10M

ideas.riskNotes: Forcing variants onto one cross-section can compromise the optimum for a specific power rating (slight efficiency give-away on outliers) — validate that the common slot geometry meets each variant's loss and torque targets. Organisational resistance from separate programme teams. Mitigate with a platform EM-design charter and per-variant CAE sign-off. No NCAP/regulatory risk; simplifies traceability under EU Battery/ELV records.

ideas.title: Adaptive servo-blanking + laser edge for near-zero cut degradation
ideas.technicalDescription: Emerging technology lever targeting E7 (cut-edge magnetic degradation) and E13 (buy-to-fly). Two convergent innovations: (1) servo-press adaptive blanking with active bridge/scrap-web minimisation and clearance control that keeps burr well under the E5 20 um limit while shrinking web/skeleton material; and (2) for prototype/low-volume or complex trial variants, laser cutting with optimised parameters (or hybrid stamp-then-laser edge finishing on tooth tips) that reduces the plastically deformed cut-edge zone versus mechanical shear, recovering some of the E7 loss. At 10M/yr full laser is too slow for the main line, but a servo-blanking main line plus targeted laser finishing of the highest-flux tooth-tip edges (where E7 degradation costs most) is a viable hybrid. The primary volume saving comes from servo-adaptive blanking cutting buy-to-fly and burr scrap; the loss recovery from reduced edge degradation enables modest stack shortening. This preserves the EM-fixed geometry (E2) and stays on an electrical-steel stamping route (E8) — no defect against stated function.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Servo progressive press with programmable ram motion enables in-cycle clearance/burr optimisation and web reduction, improving buy-to-fly and holding E5 burr. Optional laser edge-finishing cell added only for the critical tooth-tip zone — a targeted, not full-part, operation to keep cycle time viable. Capex for servo press and laser cell; running cost for laser gas/optics. Vision-based closed-loop burr/edge inspection integrates naturally. Net: better material yield, tighter burr control, and partial cut-edge loss recovery without abandoning high-volume stamping economics.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — combines yield gain with cut-edge loss recovery
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Buy-to-fly + burr-scrap reduction ~5% material plus small loss-driven stack shortening; on €0.10 material + mass

ideas.riskNotes: Laser heat-affected zone can itself degrade magnetic properties if parameters are wrong — must be tuned to be net-positive vs shear, else it becomes a defect against E7. Laser throughput limits it to targeted edges only. Servo-press adaptive control adds programming/maintenance complexity. Mitigate with HAZ metallurgical/magnetic validation and restricting laser to prototypes and critical tooth tips. No NCAP risk.
